1 NEWS FROM THE BOARD A monthly newsletter from the Ada County Board of Commissioners Welcome to the monthly newsletter from the Ada County Board of Commissioners. We are happy to share information on significant news and events in Ada County. Ryan Davidson - Commissioner Tom Dayley - Commissioner Rod Beck - Chairman ADA COUNTY LANDFILL LEARNING CENTER OPENS April 2026 NEWS FROM THE BOARD The Ada County Landfill Learning Center, which officially opened its doors Wednesday April 22, 2026, Earth Day, is the kind of place you walk into and say, “Wow!’ This 2,372 square foot functional learning center is a living example of why recycling and re-use makes sense. Almost everything in here – used to be something else. We are delighted that in the coming years this center will be a place where everyone can learn why saving space at the landfill is critically important and why it’s important for all of us to be frugal with our valuable resources. Adults, school classes, civic groups, home schoolers, scout troops and anyone else who sets up a tour will learn why little things make a big difference. Thank you to Ada County Commission Chairman Rod Beck, Commissioner Ryan Davidson and Commissioner Tom Dayley for your support. We are profoundly grateful to Ada County Landfill Director Herb Cantu and Education and Outreach Manager Rebecca Weeks. By combining top-tier landfill management with impactful, accessible education, you are not just managing waste, you are teaching us all how to live better. Thank you for creating a greener, more informed community. Interested in setting up a tour for yourself, your class, homeschoolers or civic group? SET UP A TOUR HERE or give us a call at 208-577-4790.

# Page 2^page=2
2 “The Landfill Learning Center was created to educate our community about the importance of responsible solid waste management,” said Ada County Landfill Director Herb Cantu. “It was developed to narrate the story of how innovative and sustainable solutions can be implemented to protect our valuable resources, and to create a forum for our residents, schools, and businesses to collaborate and create ideas aimed at reducing the generation of waste, identifying opportunities for reuse, and enhancing the recyclability of consumer products.” “The Ada County Landfill serves thousands of people every year without using tax dollars,” said Ada County Commission Chairman Rod Beck. “Diverting waste saves valuable materials that can be reused and repurposed thereby extending the life of our landfill. The Learning Center is an excellent resource for adults and children of all ages in our communities to better understand why this is important.” Come visit me! The Ada County Landfill hired local builders and artists to support the Learning Center’s narratives with colorful interior and exterior murals, recycled PVC decking, classroom furniture made from reclaimed 2x4s and old aluminum signs, and interior signage that features wooden lettering and reusable signs that can be easily updated.

4 ADA COUNTY OFFERING WALK-IN DRIVERS LICENSE SERVICES AT CHINDEN BLVD. DMV LOCATION No Appointment necessary The Ada County DMV location at 9115 W. Chinden Blvd. in Garden City is now a fully hybrid location. This means you can register your vehicle and get a driver’s license without making an appointment. “Making essential services convenient and efficient is a priority for our office,” said Ada County Assessor Rebecca Arnold. “Our staff serves approximately 300 customers a day at this location. We want to ensure we respect customer’s time while continuing to provide excellent service.” “Thousands of commuters pass by this location every day and we are grateful Ada Assessor Rebecca Arnold has expanded services to make getting a driver’s license even easier in Ada County,” said Ada County Commission Chairman Rod Beck. You must still make an appointment if you use the Ada County Sheriff’s Office Driver’s License office locations in Boise at 400 N. Benjamin Lane, in Meridian at 736 S. Progress Ave, and in Star at 10769 W. State Street. The Ada County Assessor’s Office has a helpful DMV Weekly Service Statistics Dashboard available where you can check the wait times at each Ada County location and find information on services. https://adacounty.id.gov/assessor/dmv- registrations-renewals-titles/

5 RECOGNIZING CHILD ABUSE AWARENESS & PREVENTION MONTH AND SEXUAL ASSAULT AWARENESS MONTH April was both Child Abuse Awareness & Prevention Month and Sexual Assault Awareness Month. Sadly, most people know someone who has experienced one or both of these profoundly destructive behaviors. Many have been directly affected themselves. The lasting impacts can stretch across generations, sending ripple effects throughout countless lives. The Ada County Commissioners were honored to recognize April as a time to contemplate both of these societal issues and to offer support to survivors. We are grateful for the outstanding Ada County professionals who support victims every day and work to prevent both. Pictured L-R: Captain Mike Ruffalo, Boise Police; Lieutenant Tim Brady, Boise Police; Heather McCarthy, Chief Civil Deputy; Nichole Solberg, Ada County Civil Prosecutor; Ada County Commissioner Ryan Davidson; Michele Bandy, Deputy Director ACVSC; Ada County Commission Chairman Rod Beck; Jan Bennetts, Ada County Prosecutor; Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley; Trina Allen, Executive Director ACVSC; Maggi Thompson, Director of Programs Family Advocates; Holly Koole, Chief of Staff; Kathryn Seebold – Executive Director Family Advocates If you or someone you know needs help, please contact the Ada County Victims Services Center (ACVSC) This one-stop facility in downtown Boise is celebrating its 20th year. Anyone experiencing interpersonal violence always has a place to go to find help. https://adacounty.id.gov/victimservices/

# Page 6^page=6
6 ASSESSOR’S OFFICE RECOGNIZES CHILD ABUSE PREVENTION MONTH A safe, nurturing, and encouraging childhood is the best gift any child can receive. Another invaluable gift is supporting efforts to prevent child abuse. The Ada County Idaho Assessor’s Office staff placed dozens of blue pinwheels along the sidewalk on Front Street near the Ada County Courthouse in April; part of the Pinwheels for Prevention campaign that recognizes April as Child Abuse Prevention Month. Child Abuse Prevention Month allows us as a community to work toward a time when no child is emotionally or physically abused, neglected, or mistreated. Thank you to the Ada County Assessor’s Office for recognizing the importance of this annual campaign.

7 ADA COUNTY’S PARK AT EXPO IDAHO Let the planting begin! We’re entering peak planting season at Ada County’s Park at Expo Idaho! One thousand trees, 3,000 shrubs, and a million-plus plugs (all native plants) will soon find their forever homes at this regional destination park set to open in late October. Ada County’s Park at Expo Idaho is taking dramatic shape right alongside the Boise River at Chinden Blvd and Glenwood Ave. It’s behind the area where you attend the Western Idaho Fair each year. People sometimes assume it’s in Garden City, since it’s surrounded by Garden City, but it’s actually in Ada County. If you look at a map of the county, you’ll notice a small (240 acre) carve-out indicating it’s part of Unincorporated Ada County. You can watch progress videos each month showing the rapid transformation on Ada County’s YouTube. WATCH THE PROGRESS VIDEOS HERE Ada County Senior Project Manager Josh Brown shows the plugs and shrubs that will soon be planted. Horse racing at what used to be known as Les Bois Park operated for decades beginning in the 1970s. While no horse racing has taken place for more than ten years this tower pays homage to the horse racing community so many people loved.

9 A SPECIAL AMERICAN FLAG FOR ADA COUNTY’S AMERICA 250 CELEBRATIONS An American Flag that flew over the United States Capitol Building in Washington, D.C. was presented to the Ada County Commissioners April 14, 2026 by Idaho Congressman Mike Simpson’s office. The ceremonial flag presentation is part of Ada County’s ongoing recognition events emphasizing the importance of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Coincidentally, this flag flew atop the United States Capitol building on Betsy Ross’s birthday, (January 1st) so it was only fitting that one of Idaho’s America 250 Spuddy Buddies, “Betsy Tot,” was also in attendance. American folklore celebrates Betsy Ross as the seamstress who sewed the first U.S. flag in 1776. As part of that flag presentation the Ada County Sheriff’s Honor Guard was on hand for the presentation of colors. The Declaration of Independence is a historic document, adopted on July 4, 1776, by the Second Continental Congress. The Declaration of Independence declared the 13 colonies’ freedom from Britain, stating the ideals of inalienable rights and self-governance. The signing of the United States Constitution, which defines the structure of the federal government, limits its powers, and guarantees the rights of American citizens, happened eleven years later in 1787. You can read the Declaration of Independence here. It takes about seven minutes. THE DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE Pictured L-R: Ada County Commissioner Ryan Davidson, Ada County Commission Chairman Rod Beck, Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley, Craig Quarterman and Chloe Angelini with Congressman Simpson’s Office, and Ada County Treasurer (and Ada County A250 Ambassador) Elizabeth Mahn.

10 How are the Declaration of Independence and the United States Constitution different? • The Declaration of Independence is a statement of intent. • The United States Constitution created a system of checks and balances so no one branch of the United States government would become too dominant. Those branches are – Legislative (Congress), Executive (President), and Judicial (Courts). The United States Constitution is the supreme law of the land, providing the legal framework for the nation. # Page 11^page=11
11 We tend to mythologize the Founding Fathers who signed the Declaration of Independence – as well we should – but its important to remember that they were just regular citizens. We now call them Statesmen, but to the newspapers of the day, they were simply politicians. What I find so fascinating is how little things have changed regarding politics in 250 years. The debates in the Continental Congress leading up to the ratification of the Declaration would be indistinguishable from a Congressional hearing today if not for the old-timey clothes. The Founding Fathers weren’t all friends. Some were rivals. Some despised other members. As someone who has been involved in politics for over 20 years, I understand their challenges all too well. Just like today, endless meetings are required to get anything done. Building consensus amongst a deliberative body can take years. Every man shows up with his own agenda. There are coalitions, and factions start to form. Endless motions are made for strategic reasons, and Robert’s Rules of Order are used like a weapon. During their debates, it became clear that there were two factions. Sam Adams, one of the more aggressive delegates, wanted to race to war with the British. Delegate Dickinson of Pennsylvania, wanted to exhaust every remedy available with the King before there was even talk of separation. The wisest delegates who wanted independence knew that in order to be successful, a unanimous vote was needed. The two factions tempered each other. While one side prevented rash action, the other side steered the debate towards declaring independence if the attempts at reconciliation failed. Many olive branch petitions were sent to the King in good faith. Delegates had to wait for months to get a response to each one. All were rejected. In the end, it became clear to all that there was only one option remaining. Live free or die. Those debates were truly a masterclass in persuasion and coalition building. It was a true miracle of history that they prevailed. The lesson for all Americans is that we too – despite all of our human frailties – can prevail as well. Our modern- day politicians can still accomplish something as great as the politicians did 250 years ago. ADA COUNTY GOVERNMENT In addition to elected offices, Ada County government includes twelve individual departments. Each department provides important services to our residents in Star, Eagle, Meridian, Boise, Garden City, Kuna, and Unincorporated Ada County. These services include law enforcement protection, emergency preparedness, election services, parks & waterways, indigent services, juvenile services, solid waste management, the Western Idaho Fair, Weed, Pest & Mosquito Abatement and more. Learn more about the services provided to you by Ada County - www.adacounty.id.gov/

12 ADA COUNTY PROSECUTOR’S OFFICE CHIEF OF STAFF HOLLY KOOLE-REBHOLTZ NAMED A 2026 HONOREE OF THE TRIBUTE TO WOMEN AND INDUSTRY (TWIN) AWARD BY THE WOMEN’S AND CHILDREN’S ALLIANCE (WCA) Now in its 33rd year, the TWIN program recognizes professional women across the Treasure Valley who demonstrate excellence in their fields and make significant contributions in executive, managerial, and professional roles. The award also highlights organizations that support the advancement of women and foster opportunities for leadership. Holly Koole-Rebholtz serves as Chief of Staff for the Ada County Prosecutor’s Office and has been a deputy prosecutor in Ada County since 2006. She graduated from the University of Idaho College of Law in 2005 and began her career clerking for the Honorable John Mitchell in Coeur d’Alene before joining the Ada County Prosecutor’s Office. The Women’s and Children’s Alliance has presented TWIN awards for more than three decades, recognizing nearly 1,400 women who demonstrate professional excellence while contributing to the strength and vitality of the community. Congratulations Holly!

13 Coming up next month, you’re about to see an epic one-month transformation of Ada County’s Park at Expo Idaho as more than 1,000 trees, 3,000 shrubs, and a million-plus plugs (all native plants) get planted. The onsite nursery at the park is ready, in May the actual digging begins! Interesting Factoid: Balled and burlapped (B&B) trees are field-grown, mature trees harvested with their root ball and native soil intact, then wrapped in burlap and secured with a wire basket. This method protects roots during transport, allowing for larger, more established trees Also coming up – May 19, 2026 is the 2026 Primary Election. Primaries are held in even-numbered years on the third Tuesday in May in Idaho. Those candidates who receive the most votes during the primary election go on to run in the general election in November. We’ll share voter turnout COMING UP!
